title: Man Wins First-of-Its-Kind Religious Exemption from Mandatory AI Use at Work
content:
Man granted first-of-its-kind religious exemption against mandatory AI use at work — Humanist argues that offloading his thinking to LLMs violates his beliefs, Title VII accommodation protects employee
David Durman says that he's unwilling to outsource his thinking to AI tools.
David Durman, a research administrator at the University of Kentucky (UK), has successfully argued that using AI violates his beliefs as a humanist and has received Title VII religious accommodation from university officials not to use the technology. According to the Religion News Service (RNS), Durman believes in "the human part of life," which includes making his own decisions. However, he says that when the UK asked its employees to use AI, he felt that doing so would mean outsourcing his thinking to tools like ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot, thus violating his deeply held beliefs.
“The process and work involved in thinking through situations, through my work, through my ethics, through the way I handle other people, is a key component in being able to develop myself as a moral person,” Durman told RNS in an interview. “And offloading that labor, regardless of whether it’s taxing or not, is undercutting my ability to be a moral actor.” Because of this, the research administrator was granted a Title VII exemption under the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibited employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, and national origin. While humanism is often a non-religious philosophy or a worldview, federal courts have ruled that it qualifies as a religion.
The American Humanist Association (AHA) assisted Durman with his request for the accommodation. “This is the first of its kind at the AHA and for humanism generally to exempt those who see AI use as flying in the face of their freedom of conscience,” AHA staff attorney Alexandria Huiskens said to RNS. She also added, “For us, humanism is a comprehensive way of life. It’s built on inherent worth and dignity, and everyone should have room to exercise this comprehensive way of life at work the same way Christians do, or Muslims do.”
It should be noted that while anyone can request a Title VII exemption, it will only be granted if the applicant has a deep moral conviction that could count as an article of faith. Aside from that, the law also states that the request should not place an “undue hardship on the employer’s business.” So, even though Durman is no longer personally required to use AI tools for his tasks, he is still expected to attend meetings and cooperate with colleagues who use AI or to submit materials to AI tools, as needed.
AI use in corporate settings has been one of the biggest questions ever since LLMs exploded in popularity with ChatGPT. While AI proponents have said that the technology would increase productivity multiple times, reports say that corporate America, except for Big Tech, is not seeing any financial returns. Even so, about half of all U.S. employees now use AI one way or another at work, even as many executives remain uncertain about AI’s return on investment. But as for Durman, he says that the fact that Americans are already thinking about the impact of AI is a good thing, and that he hopes that his story would help others who’d rather not be forced to use the technology.

report.summary: A University of Kentucky research administrator won the first known Title VII religious accommodation exempting him from mandatory workplace AI use.
report.background: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 bars employment discrimination based on religion and requires reasonable accommodation unless it imposes undue hardship. Courts have treated deeply held secular humanism as a religion for some purposes, which gave Durman a legal path. The case arrives as employers push generative AI into everyday work—ChatGPT, Copilot and similar tools—while debate continues over productivity gains, job quality and worker agency. About half of U.S. employees reportedly use AI at work, yet many executives remain unsure about ROI. That tension between top-down adoption and individual conscience is creating new workplace-policy questions.
key_points: David Durman, a research administrator at the University of Kentucky, received a Title VII religious accommodation allowing him not to use AI tools that the university encouraged or required. The American Humanist Association says it is the first such case for humanism and for the organization.

Durman argues that outsourcing thinking to LLMs such as ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot undermines his ability to develop as a moral person. He frames decision-making and ethical reasoning as central to his humanist beliefs, not merely a workplace preference.

The exemption is narrow. Title VII accommodations must reflect a sincerely held belief and must not cause undue hardship; Durman can still be expected to attend meetings, cooperate with AI-using colleagues, and submit materials to AI systems when needed.

The case tests how far religion extends in workplace tech mandates. Federal courts have recognized humanism as a religion in some contexts, but each request turns on sincerity and employer hardship, so it is a precedent signal rather than a blanket right to refuse AI.

It also highlights a growing worker-agency debate. Some programmers say generative AI reduces insight and enjoyment, while others use it selectively for code review or debugging—showing adoption is not all-or-nothing.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the accommodation signals that mandatory adoption can trigger civil-rights and HR risk, especially where AI is framed as replacing judgment rather than assisting it. Developers should expect demand for explainable, controllable tools that preserve user agency, auditability, and clear human-review workflows—not just productivity features. Employers may need formal opt-out processes, alternative task assignments, and documentation showing no undue hardship. For regular users, the case offers a template for conscientious objection, but the bar is high: a sincerely held belief, legal support, and a narrow accommodation. It does not create a general right to avoid AI, but it does push workplace AI policies toward negotiation, transparency, and respect for dissent.
report.tools: Follow ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot, the tools named in the case, plus workplace-governance resources: EEOC Title VII guidance, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and AHA materials on humanism. For open-source follow-up, look at AI-policy template repositories on GitHub and model-transparency approaches such as model cards. No dedicated open-source tool grants AI exemptions; the practical work is policy design, documentation, and opt-out workflows.
